arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Lamken argued that the Commissioner has long construed the program to require two conditions for disability.
He stated that a claimant must be unable to do their previous work to qualify.
Mr. Alter argued that the Commissioner is acting against its own theme of providing remedies for disabled individuals.
He asserted that Congress intended to separate the analysis of previous work from other work.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the legal standard for determining disability under the Social Security program. It asks how courts must weigh a claimant's ability to perform previous work versus other work.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The Commissioner seeks a ruling that denies benefits if the claimant can do other work.
The claimant seeks a ruling that grants benefits if she cannot do her previous job.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The Commissioner argues that disability requires an inability to do both previous and other work.
The claimant argues that Congress intended to separate the analysis of previous work from other work.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: How must courts distinguish between the ability to do previous work and other work?
Does the statutory language require a specific separation between these two steps?

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the threshold for receiving federal disability benefits. It determines how many Americans can access financial support when they lose their ability to work. The outcome shapes the scope of the social safety net for workers with impairments.
